title: Sauerbraten
subtitle: German sweet-sour pot roast
excerpt: Sauerbraten is one of Germany's most celebrated dishes. Beef is marinated for 24 hours in a wine and vinegar bath, then slow-braised until tender. The sauce is rich, tangy, and gently sweet.
sourceNotes: Sauerbraten is considered one of Germany's national dishes. It dates back centuries and was traditionally made with horse meat. The long marinade tenderises tough cuts and creates the dish's characteristic tangy sweetness.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the cooked beef in its sauce for up to 3 months.

content.text: Sauerbraten takes patience, but most of that time is hands-off. The 24-hour marinade does the hard work. The result is deeply flavoured beef in a sauce that balances vinegar sharpness with gentle sweetness.
Combine vinegar, wine, sliced onion, carrot, bay, cloves, allspice, and pepper in a large bowl or zip-lock bag. Add the beef. Cover and refrigerate for 24 hours, turning once if possible.
Remove the beef and pat it dry. Strain the marinade and reserve it. Discard the solids.
Heat oil in a cast-iron skillet over a high heat. Sear the beef on all sides until well browned, about 8 minutes total. Transfer to a heavy pot or casserole.
Pour the strained marinade and beef stock over the beef. Bring to a gentle simmer. Cover and braise on a low heat for 2.5 to 3 hours, turning once, until the beef is very tender.
Remove the beef and rest on a board. Strain the cooking liquid into a saucepan. Bring to a simmer.
Mix flour with a little cold water to a smooth paste. Whisk into the sauce. Add brown sugar. Simmer 5 minutes, stirring, until the sauce thickens. Taste and adjust seasoning.
Slice the beef and return to the sauce to warm through. Serve with potato dumplings, spaetzle, or mashed potato.

items.fix: Add 1-2 tsp brown sugar and simmer for 5 minutes

content.text: Sauerbraten is most strongly associated with the Rhineland, where it is made with horse meat in the traditional version. Across Germany it is a Sunday roast staple. It is served at the table with potato dumplings (Kartoffelkloesse) or spaetzle to soak up the sauce. It tastes better the next day, reheated gently.
